content: Sentinel node assessment is a diagnostic method used to evaluate the involvement of groin lymph nodes in vulval cancer. Vulval cancer is typically managed with wide local excision and removal of groin lymph nodes (inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy, or IFL) on one or both sides, depending on the tumor's location. However, this surgical procedure is associated with significant morbidity. Since lymph node metastases occur in approximately 30% of women with early-stage vulval cancer, accurately predicting lymph node involvement could help reduce the extent of surgery and, consequently, the associated morbidity. The sentinel node assessment technique involves the use of traceable agents to identify the sentinel lymph nodes, which are the first nodes to which cancer cells are likely to spread from the primary tumor. Once identified, these sentinel nodes are surgically removed and subjected to histological examination to determine the presence of metastases. This method has been successfully applied to other types of cancers and has been evaluated in vulval cancer using various tracing agents. However, it remains unclear which tracing agent or combination of agents provides the highest diagnostic accuracy. The objective of this study was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of different techniques using traceable agents for sentinel lymph node assessment in women with FIGO stage IB or higher vulval cancer. The study also aimed to investigate potential sources of variability in the results. A systematic search of databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane trial registers, was conducted to identify relevant studies published up to early 2013. Studies were included if they evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of sentinel node assessment (using traceable agents and histological examination) compared to the histological examination of groin lymph nodes following complete IFL. The studies needed to provide sufficient data to construct two-by-two tables for analysis. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for inclusion, assessed their methodological quality using the QUADAS-2 tool, and extracted data. A meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled sensitivity values for the different techniques. A total of 34 studies involving 1,614 women and approximately 2,396 groins were included. The overall methodological quality of the studies was moderate. The studies employed various tracing techniques, including blue dye alone (3 studies), technetium alone (8 studies), a combination of blue dye and technetium (13 studies), and mixed or inconsistent combinations of these techniques (10 studies). Histological examination of sentinel nodes was primarily performed using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, with some studies also employing immunohistochemical (IHC) staining, with or without ultrastaging. One study used reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis, while three studies did not describe their histological methods. The pooled sensitivity estimates for the different techniques were as follows: Blue dye alone: 94% (68 women; 95% confidence interval [CI] 69% to 99%) Technetium alone: 93% (149 women; 95% CI 89% to 96%) Combined blue dye and technetium: 95% (390 women; 95% CI 89% to 97%) Mixed tests: 91% (679 women; 95% CI 71% to 98%) The negative predictive values (NPVs) for all techniques exceeded 95%. Sentinel node detection rates, which reflect the ability of the test to identify a sentinel node, were 82% for blue dye alone, 95% for mixed tests, 96% for technetium alone, and 98% for the combined technique. The clinical implications of these findings were estimated for 100 women undergoing sentinel node assessment, assuming a 30% prevalence of groin metastases. For the combined or technetium-only techniques, 1 to 2 women with groin metastases might be missed (95% CI 1 to 3). For mixed tests, 3 women might be missed (95% CI 1 to 9). The wide confidence intervals for blue dye and mixed tests suggest a higher likelihood of missing women with groin metastases. In conclusion, there is minimal difference in diagnostic accuracy between the technetium-only and combined techniques. However, the combined technique may reduce the number of missed cases of groin metastases compared to technetium alone. Blue dye alone appears to be associated with a higher rate of missed cases. Sentinel node assessment using technetium-based techniques could reduce the need for IFL by 70% in women with early vulval cancer. However, it remains uncertain how the survival outcomes of women with negative sentinel nodes compare to those undergoing standard IFL. Conducting a randomized controlled trial to compare sentinel node dissection with IFL poses methodological and ethical challenges. Therefore, additional observational data on survival outcomes in women with early vulval cancer are needed.
